name: George Comninos
comments: Started on 40m. I have been very excited about my active loop antenna, which is also on the Airspy Spserver network. Now I can use it to listen on my Hermes Lite 2 SDR as well (and switch it to public facing users on the Airspy Discovery HF+ when not in the shack). Spent the day with my mate Tommy VK2IR winding a 50 ohm to 75 ohm UNUN for his upcoming DX-pedition to Tonga? ...I think?? My HF amplifier now has some temperature coefficient control (diodes in the bias line) to compensate for quiescent current taking off when the FETS heat up, so no SMOKE (so far??) and 40+ watts. I LOVE CW dit dit.
caption: The "Alien Loop" with vertical in background

name: Adam
comments:
Once again, the afternoon storms caused some havoc. I had an S8 noise floor with crashes but managed a 20 minute QSO with Merv in Ballarat before his signal faded under the noise and crashes. We managed to end the QSO gracefully and not just disappear. A later QSO with Manny was a little easier, the crashes had subsided and he was a solid signal, But I still suffered from the S8 suburban smog. Both QSO's were good practice and really made me concentrate.

On another note, I've been trying to make at least one QSO a day on CW since late September and for the most part I've succeeded. It's not really a challenge, just something I want to do. Where I've missed a day I've made two contacts to cover it. Most contacts have been on 10m into the United States. So the weak signals and fading have been testing me.

All reports of 10m being dead are greatly exaggerated ;-)

name: Willie
qth: JO30WJ - Montabaur - Half way between Frankfurt in the south and Cologne in the north.
comments:
I strained myself and so I had back pain. For that reason I could not go portable and set up an antenna. Instead I used the 1/4 wave vertical with elevated radials right here at home and used 100 W. I called for a while and was about to give up, when VK3DBD, David answered. We had a nice QSO - even though there was QSB. I am not an experienced operator, so I had to struggle with the conditions. But when looking on what I had noted down, I saw, I got more than expected - even the QTH, as I proved later - on the first view I thought there were only mistakes in my copy  "yackadandah", but it wasn't to bad: "YACKANDANDAH" :))
So I am looking forward to the next DXperiments.
caption: A very simple homebrew antenna. 1/4 wave, two radials. 3D-printed and sealed with hot glue.

name: Adrian
worked40: VK3ASR, VK2WP, VK3AVA, VK3WOW, VK5GG, VK3EST
comments:
High levels of QRN S9+20, CW QSOs are still possible when using a separate receive antenna, in this case a terminated loop without a pre-amp also with a selective CW speaker system which minimizes, static crashes.
The TS-520s has a 700Hz CW offset BFO note, when matched with a 700Hz CW speaker it makes for an enjoyable CW experience. CW QSOs are practical in high levels of thunderstorm QRN.

name: Mark
qth: Camping at Dalmeny on the South Coast of NSW
heard40: VK2WF, VK5IP, VK5AO, VK3ACU, VK3RU, VK3DRQ, VK3ADX, VK4IM, VK4PN, VK6NW, VK3DRQ
heardOther: IU4FLS@20, VK3XU@20, VK3DBD@20, DL3YZ@20, VK3DRQ@20, DJ9FM@20
comments:
This week we were at Dalmeny, a lovely small spot just North of Narooma on the NSW far South Coast.  In the wind in the morning I had struggled to put up my 6.5m squid pole and ZS6BKW doublet on our caravan;  but  I gave it away... with all the vans spaced millimetres apart, the consequences of a support failure just didn't balance the rewards.  So in the afternoon, I took Elizabeth's Forester to a quiet part of the caravan park and put the doublet up there, with the help of a couple of tall trees spaced 50m apart.  So I was nicely set-up for an evening's fun.

[15m]

Jordan VK3ACU reported via our CQQRS WhatsApp groups that 15m was hopping earlier;  however, when I listened for Edi DO2EMR using the VK5PH KiwiSDRs at Ironstone Range, nothing at all was to be heard.

[20m]

Signals from Europe were marginal.  Fausto was RSN 348 in QSB and static crashes, but he was busy chatting to VKs.  By the time there was a gap to try some QRP action, Fausto didn't hear my 10W.

Meanwhile I happened to look out the window of the car;  I was parked next to the main road through town, opposite the local fish and chippery.  Hopping down the centre of the road was a large male kangaroo.  When I've lived overseas, a frequent question asked by locals was whether kangaroos could be seen in cities;  pity I wasn't quick enough with the camera.  Of course, where we live in rural Australia, there are usually kangaroos on our road, in our property etc... they're a real menace for drivers (a year or two back, our neighbour SWL-Jack had a roo jump through their windscreen when driving down their driveway!  Anyway, back to the net!

Mike DL3YZ came up and was RSN 318;  Edi DJ9FM was also only RSN 118 (I heard the occasional tone, but not enough to make out any characters).  Neither of our German mates could hear my QRP of course.

[40m]

40m was horrible to listen to;  we had thunderstorms inland from us and out to sea - the lines on the two Apps I checked ran from Victoria to Queensland.  Not only were the crashes continuous, one after the other, but in my receiver they often combined to sound more like continuous tearing or crumpling of paper.  However, despite the S8-9 QRN, band conditions were good - and there was a bunch of really strong signals from our team to listen enjoy.

I hooked up with Kevin VK3KEV who was put activating a Park;  solid RSN 599 (ie S9 of noise, but S9+ of signal.  Wal, VK2WP up at Bathurst was similarly strong.

After 20m and dinner, I returned - the static crashes were still S9... meaning my RSN reports sounded awfully like RSTs.  I hooked up with George VK2AOE at Kogarah who was using his vertical antenna on transmit, and his active loop on receive.  I really enjoyed our hour-long chat, including the news that George had recently worked a French station using his active loop.

After George, I had a brief chat to Andrew, VK2DA;  Andrew is also VK1DA, but was using his remote station at Yass (near where I live) and hence his VK2 call.  I completed the session with a chat to Paul VK3KLE at Stawell who was QRP using what he called a "ground wire" antenna.  Hope we learn more about that from Paul in the future.  As often happens, every time Paul sent me my report.... static crash, QSB dip, etc.  I think I took three or four "PSE RPT AGN? RPT? RPT?" with replies to finally get it!

Through the QSO and for previous half hour, I'd dropped my great little stubby YA1860 key (thank you Richard VK6HRC) off my knee in the dark.  Each time I picked it up, when it was my turn to transmit, the transmitter wouldn't key up.  Several seconds of Vs were required before it started working.  I thought one of the wires had broken (it was dark in the car, so I couldn't easily see what was going on);  however, when it happened every time I figured that it may have been the salt spray from the ocean 200m to my right that was causing the contacts on the key to form a layer of corrosion.  Boy our many ex-maritime radio operators must have had fun with this sort of thing!

After only one QSO on 80m I came back up to 40m and was pleased to hear CQQRS still going.  As usual, Wayne VK6NW at Bridgetown was coming in nicely here;  I don't know what it is about Wayne's antennas, but he has a consistently good signal on 40m when the band opens.  Wayne was enjoying a chat with Sava VK4PN at Mount Ommaney, but by the time they finished, I think he'd dropped down a bit and I was pretty pooped, so gave it away for the night.

[80m]

Surprisingly, 80m was actually less noisy than 40m;  S7 static crashes rather than S8-9.  Adrian VK2WF up at Talong was really struggling to hear me, despite his S9 signal here.

So thank you to everyone who braved the dire QRN this week - very much appreciated by me, and by many listeners I reckon.
caption: Feedline to ZS6BKW doublet up 6m at Dalmeny; Not a kangaroo in the street, one of three emus on the beach; Paul reckoned I should work harder to keep the key from falling off my knee. Easier said than done in the dark.

name: Sava
comments: All up I had only 30 minutes on air. QRN was horrendous due to a monster storm stretching from the Gold Coast to central Queensland mine fields. BOM radar showed plenty of red and dark brown patches indicating massive downpours and of course lightening galore. 80 m was deserted and unworkable 40 m was a bit better so called few CQ QRS not expecting much but Armin vk2gas came back with a strong signal, RSN 599 + very hard to chat between constant crashes but we struggled for a while. It was almost net closing time when we finished QSO and I checked Ironside SDR. There was a reasonable trace  couple of KHz above my frequency so I tuned in and had a quick listen, it was vk6nw buried in QRN. I called him and he came back and  gave me RSN of 566 which wasn't  bad I gave Wayne 579 + but again copy was very poor at my end. We struggled with the QSO well pass the net finishing time.

name: Paul
comments:
Thanks for the nice qrs qso Mark. I was on my ten tech tonight. Just finished reseting the carrier osc to fillter out rx bellow about 250 hz on both filters. Just in time for the awful qrn static.

Try not to drop the key off your lap again, less coffee and and arvo nap perhaps next time.

I was using a ground wire ant and military tuner. Rated for about 25 watts. It will tune a short vertical or ground trail ant from mf to 20m. Will go higher up with a shorter radiator. Very handy pice of old military kit.

As we just proved. Good enough for cw state to state in poor conditions.
